text:
In late August 1854, a terrible illness arrived in Soho, a crowded, working-class district of London, and the disease was cholera, which strikes with brutal speed: violent vomiting and diarrhoea drain the body of water, the skin turns blue and shrunken, and a healthy person can be dead within a day. Within three days of the outbreak's start, more than a hundred people living near Broad Street had died. Within a week, hundreds more had followed, and many families fled the neighbourhood, leaving shuttered houses behind them.

At the time, almost nobody understood what caused cholera. The dominant belief among doctors and officials was the miasma theory, that disease spread through foul air rising from rotting waste, marshes and filthy streets, a sensible-sounding idea in a city that stank. But a physician named John Snow was not convinced. Snow was a respected doctor who had pioneered the use of anaesthetics, even administering chloroform to Queen Victoria during childbirth, and he lived close to Soho and had been thinking about cholera for years. In 1849 he had published a short essay arguing that the disease was not breathed in but swallowed, and that it travelled through contaminated water. Few people took the idea seriously.

The Broad Street outbreak gave Snow a chance to test it, and he did something that now seems obvious but was unusual then: he went door to door, collecting facts. He obtained the official list of the dead from the local registrar and began visiting the homes of the victims, asking where each household got its drinking water. Most of London's water came from rivers, but in Soho many people relied on public pumps in the street, drawing water from wells beneath them. Snow noticed that the deaths clustered tightly around one pump, the one on Broad Street.

To make the pattern plain, he drew a map, marking each death with a small black bar stacked at the address where it had occurred on a street plan of the district. The bars piled up thickly around the Broad Street pump and thinned out with distance. It was a striking picture, though Snow was careful to note that it was not enough on its own, since a cluster might be a coincidence, or might simply reflect where the most people lived.

So he looked harder at the exceptions, and this is where his investigation became persuasive. A workhouse near the pump, home to hundreds of residents, had suffered remarkably few deaths, and Snow discovered that it had its own well and did not use the Broad Street pump. A brewery on the same street had no cases at all among its workers. The men there were given free beer and, as it turned out, they also had their own water supply; beer was brewed with boiled water, which would have killed whatever caused the disease, though no one yet knew why.

Even more telling were the cases that seemed to contradict his theory, because some people who lived far from Broad Street had died, and Snow traced them one by one. A woman in Hampstead, miles away, had died of cholera, and on inquiring he learned that she had once lived in Soho and liked the taste of the Broad Street water so much that she had it carried to her house each day. Her niece, who drank the same water, died as well, while other residents of her neighbourhood stayed well. Some children who attended a school near the pump and drank from it had also fallen ill, while those who had not drunk it escaped.

By early September, Snow was confident enough to approach the local board of guardians, the officials responsible for the parish, and on 7 September he urged them to act. They agreed, somewhat reluctantly, to remove the pump's handle so that no one could draw water from it. The outbreak was already declining by then, since many residents had fled or died, so critics later argued that removing the handle made little real difference, and that debate continues among historians. But the gesture became symbolic of a new way of thinking about disease.

The final piece of the puzzle came afterwards, when a local clergyman, Henry Whitehead, who had been sceptical of Snow's ideas, began his own inquiries among his parishioners. Whitehead discovered that the first known victim, an infant girl who lived at 40 Broad Street, had fallen ill just before the outbreak, and that her mother had washed the child's soiled nappies and tipped the water into a cesspool just yards from the well. Examination of the well later showed that its lining was cracked, allowing sewage to seep in. Whitehead, once a doubter, became Snow's ally.

Snow died in 1858, still largely unrecognised, and the official inquiry into the outbreak rejected his conclusions. Yet his method of mapping cases, comparing the sick with the healthy and chasing down exceptions laid the foundation for modern epidemiology. A few years later, London built its great sewer system, and cholera retreated. The handle, in a sense, had been removed from the city's most dangerous pump.
